title: Two Strings
directAnswer: Two strings share a common substring if and only if they share at least one common character — because any single shared letter is itself a length-1 common substring. So you never need to enumerate substrings at all: build a set (or 26-slot boolean array) of the characters in one string and scan the other for any hit. Return "YES" on the first shared character, "NO" if none. O(n + m) time, O(1) space.

seen = set(s1)
for ch in s2:
    if ch in seen: return "YES"
return "NO"

Never enumerate substrings — that's the trap that turns an O(n) problem into O(n²·m).
Return the string `"YES"` / `"NO"`, not a boolean — match the prompt's output spec exactly.

remember.takeaway: The whole puzzle is a misdirection: it says 'substring' but a single shared letter already is one. Reducing 'common substring exists?' to 'character sets intersect?' is the insight that turns a brute-force enumeration into one linear pass.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you notice that a length-1 substring counts, collapsing the problem to a set-intersection check, instead of mechanically generating every substring.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Enumerating all substrings of one string and searching for each inside the other — correct but O(n²·m), and a signal you missed the single-character insight.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say out loud: 'A shared substring of length 1 is enough, so I just need to know if the two character sets intersect.' Then note the 26-letter alphabet gives O(1) space.

problemStatement:
Given two strings, determine whether they share a **common substring**. A substring may be as small as a single character.

For each pair return the string `"YES"` if the two strings share any common substring, and `"NO"` if they do not.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters only
understanding: Because a substring can have length 1, 's1 and s2 share a common substring' is exactly equivalent to 's1 and s2 share at least one common letter'. If even one character appears in both, that character alone is a valid common substring. So we reduce the question to a membership test over a small alphabet.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the common substring have to be longer than one character?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — a single shared character is itself a length-1 substring, which is what makes this an O(n) set-intersection problem rather than a DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters can appear?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase a–z only, so a fixed 26-element boolean array gives O(1) extra space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to return the substring or just yes/no?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the strings "YES" or "NO". We only test existence, never reconstruct the match.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the strings be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Constraints say length ≥ 1, but if one were empty the answer is trivially "NO" — no characters to share.

examples.explanation: They share 'o' and 'l'. Either one alone is a common substring of length 1.
{h, i} and {w, o, r, l, d} are disjoint — no shared character, so no common substring.
'a' is in both — a single shared character is enough.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to show you can model the literal question, then immediately note it's wasteful because a single character already settles it.
hints: The literal reading is 'is some substring of s1 also a substring of s2?'. What's the most direct way to test that?
Generate every substring of s1 with two nested indices (i, j), then check whether s2 contains it.
Each `contains` check is itself O(m), and there are O(n²) substrings — so this is O(n²·m). Correct, but a red flag that you've missed something simpler.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n(n+1)/2 ≈ n²/2 substrings of s1; testing each for membership in s2 with a naive `contains` is O(m). Total O(n²·m). Building substrings costs up to O(n) space each.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the prompt word-for-word: for every substring of `s1`, ask whether it appears anywhere in `s2`. Two nested indices `i ≤ j` slice out `s1[i:j]`, and `s2.contains(...)` answers membership.

**Why this is the literal-but-wrong-sized first attempt.** The question literally says 'common substring', so the mechanical response is to produce all substrings and test each one. It returns the correct answer — the first substring found in `s2` proves a shared substring exists.

**Why it is enormously wasteful.** You're checking substrings of length 1, 2, 3, … but if *any* of them matches, a length-1 piece of it already matched. So all the work spent on longer substrings is redundant. The nested generation alone is O(n²), and each membership probe adds another O(m) factor — for `n = m = 10⁵` that's astronomically slow.

**The realisation that shrinks it.** If `s1[i:j]` is a substring of `s2`, then its first character `s1[i]` is also a substring of `s2`. So you only ever needed to test single characters. That observation is the entire optimal algorithm — open with brute force, then collapse it.
approaches.insight: Every multi-character common substring contains a single common character. So the existence question for substrings of any length is equivalent to the existence question for length-1 substrings — which is just set intersection.

approaches.name: Character-Set Intersection (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — phrase it as 'a single shared letter is a common substring, so I just intersect the character sets'.
hints: If any single character is shared, you're done. What data structure answers 'is this character present?' in O(1)?
Record every character of s1 in a set (or a boolean[26]). Then scan s2 once.
The moment a character of s2 is already in the set, return YES. If you finish the scan with no hit, return NO.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the set is O(n). Scanning s2 is O(m). Each membership test is O(1). Total O(n + m). The set holds at most 26 distinct lowercase letters, so space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Record the alphabet of `s1` in a set, then walk `s2` and return `"YES"` at the first character that's already present.

**Why this is correct and complete.** From the brute-force insight, a common substring of any length implies a common *character*. So the two strings share a substring exactly when their character sets intersect. Storing `s1`'s characters and probing each character of `s2` tests precisely that intersection.

**Why it's O(1) space, not O(n).** The alphabet is fixed at 26 lowercase letters. A `boolean[26]` (or a Python set that can hold at most 26 distinct letters) never grows with input length, so the extra memory is constant. Say this explicitly — interviewers love the 'small fixed alphabet → O(1)' observation.

**Why scan s2 lazily.** We return on the very first shared character. There's no benefit to building a second full set for `s2`; a single streaming pass with early exit is both simplest and fastest in the common case where a match appears early.

**Build the set from the shorter string** if you want to shave constant-factor memory — correctness is unchanged, but the set is then bounded by the smaller alphabet.
approaches.insight: This is the canonical 'pay O(1) memory to buy O(1) membership tests' trade, identical in spirit to Two Sum's complement lookup. The cleverness isn't the data structure — it's realising the substring question was a length-1 question in disguise.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Enumerating substrings instead of characters
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Any common substring contains a common character, so testing single characters is sufficient. The substring loop is O(n²·m) for no benefit.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning a boolean instead of YES/NO
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The prompt's output contract is the literal strings. Returning True/False fails the grader even though the logic is right.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Heavyweight set for a tiny alphabet
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only 26 lowercase letters are possible, so a boolean[26] is O(1) and cache-friendly; a HashSet adds boxing and hashing overhead.

patternNote: Set-membership / character-set intersection over a fixed alphabet. Whenever a string question only needs 'does any element appear in both?', collapse it to a set intersection in O(n + m). The trap here is wording: 'substring' sounds like DP, but a length-1 match makes it a single linear pass.
